title: Why the serve and the return decide so many points
seo_title: Table tennis serve and receive tactics explained
description: Why the serve and return of serve shape table tennis points: short and long serves, the third ball, how to return each serve and what the research shows.
summary: Most rallies at a good level are decided in the first few shots, and the serve is the one you fully control. Here is how servers set up the point and how receivers fight back.
key_points: You serve two points in a row, then your opponent does; from 10-10 you take one each.
In one study of elite European men's matches, 11.6% of points were won by the serve itself and 22.4% with the server's next shot.
A short serve, one that would bounce twice on the far side, can't be looped because the table is in the way.
Attack long serves; vary your return against short ones with short pushes, long pushes and flicks.
Read the serve from the bat at contact, decide early and commit to your shot.
body: The serve is the one shot in table tennis your opponent cannot influence, so a good server can decide what kind of ball comes back and be ready to attack it. The return of serve, or receive, is the receiver's first chance to take that control away. At a good level many points are won or lost in those first two or three shots, which is why players spend hours practising serves and returns that last a second or two.

Under the laws, the serve changes hands after every two points. If the score reaches 10-10, each player serves one point in turn until someone leads by two. Over a game you serve about half the points, so being better on your own serve than your opponent is on theirs is usually enough to win. The rules on how to serve are strict: the ball must be tossed at least 16cm without spin and must stay in the receiver's view. Our guide to [legal serves](/guide/legal-serve-rules.html) explains them.

Researchers who analysed 1,466 points from elite European men's matches, between players in the European top 30, found that 11.6% of points were won directly by the serve, and another 22.4% with the server's next shot, the third ball. Only 1.5% of points were lost to service faults. The serve they saw most often was a short forehand serve, used 76.9% of the time.

The server does not always win, though. A 2023 study of Greek league matches cited earlier research from the 2015 European Games, where match winners won 60.6% of the points on their own serve and losers only 46.7%. The same study found the winners' returns of serve were successful up to 10 percentage points more often than the losers'. The receive matters as much as the serve.

Serves are described by length. The American coach Larry Hodges, writing for Butterfly, defines a short serve as one that, if left, "would bounce twice on the far side of the table". Its great advantage is that it "cannot be looped like a deep serve because the table is in the way": the receiver cannot swing freely at it. He suggests serving so that the second bounce would land near the end line, which makes the ball hard both to attack and to drop short.

Each spin has its trade-off. A short backspin serve "is tricky to attack" but can be pushed back heavy or short; a short sidespin-topspin serve is awkward to return, especially on the forehand; and with a serve that has almost no spin, "the opponent can't use your spin against you". Hodges adds that short serves work best when mixed with long ones, so the receiver cannot simply wait over the net. Our guide to [spin](/guide/spin-in-table-tennis-explained.html) explains what each spin does.

The point of most serves is the third ball: the server's first shot after the return. A server who knows which returns their serve is likely to produce can be in position to loop or smash it. That is why good players plan serve and third ball together, and why the same serve can be followed by very different attacks depending on where the return goes.

Hodges's rule for long serves is simple: attack them. "Ideally, you should loop any serve that is long." Against a short serve with topspin or sidespin, a flick, a short attacking stroke played over the table, is usually the answer. Attacked at a reasonable pace, he says, even heavy sidespin moves the ball only "a foot or less", about 30cm.

Short backspin is harder. The general rule is variation: learn to push short, push long and flick. Pushing long is the easiest return, but it hands the server a ball to loop, and "the most common receive at the higher levels is a short push", kept "quick, low, with good backspin, to a wide angle". At the top, the backhand banana flick, a flick played with sidespin and topspin, now lets players attack even short serves. Massimo Costantini, then the ITTF's high-performance manager, wrote in 2019 that it had begun in China about 10 years earlier and that the short or long push on the return "is now part of the past" at that level.
## Reading the serve and choosing a return

Watch the server's bat at contact rather than the ball. Table Tennis Scotland's coaching advice is to "look for the serve drifting long first", because a long serve is the one you can attack, and then, having read the spin, to "decide and commit to the shot".

Do not become predictable. Hodges divides returns into passive (long pushes or soft topspin), neutral (short pushes or a well-placed flick) and aggressive (looping long serves and flicking short ones). He suggests learning all three, specialising in two and keeping the third as a surprise.

Serve practice needs only a box of balls and an empty table: work on a few serves until you can put them short, long and to either corner with spin you choose. For the receive, ask a club partner to serve the same serve repeatedly while you try each return, then mix them up. If your serves keep being attacked, check your style of play first in our guide to [playing styles](/guide/table-tennis-playing-styles.html), and look up any unfamiliar terms in the [glossary](/guide/table-tennis-glossary.html).
